details: 🔍 Review comparing pediatric PENTEC with adult QUANTEC and HyTEC: content, oversight, support, scope, literature-review method
🔍 PENTEC aims to refine dose-volume NTCP relationships in pediatric cancer survivors

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Narrative comparison of **PENTEC** with the adult **QUANTEC** and **HyTEC** efforts across content, oversight, support, scope and literature-review method, followed by organ-specific pediatric findings.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: Child vs adult risk is **similar** for brain necrosis, optic apparatus, parotid and liver; **greater** for neurocognition, cerebrovascular and breast lactation; **less** for ovary; **perhaps slightly less** for lung. Maldevelopment of musculoskeletal tissue, teeth, breast and reproductive organs is relevant primarily only in children.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: QUANTEC and HyTEC remain the adult reference for conventional and hypofractionated constraints; PENTEC is the pediatric counterpart, and this paper is the first framing of where the two sets diverge by organ.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents pediatric and adolescent cancer survivors whose normal tissues received RT. Does not represent a validated age-adjusted constraint set for direct substitution into adult or pediatric planning.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Comparisons are **confounded by treatment paradigm** (cancer type, dose, fields, chemo), and the optimal age model (continuous vs groupings) is unresolved.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: Age and developmental status modify risk in organ-specific directions, so a single age cutoff for applying adult or pediatric constraints is not supported. The authors state further work is needed to define how age shapes risk.

studies.interpretation:
The useful frame here is that age is not a uniform risk multiplier. A common clinical shortcut treats children as categorically more radiosensitive and applies adult QUANTEC or HyTEC constraints with an informal safety margin. This synthesis argues against that heuristic in both directions. For some endpoints (brain necrosis, optic apparatus, parotid, liver) the pediatric and adult risk appear similar, so a blanket tightening of constraints may cost target coverage without buying toxicity reduction. For others (neurocognition, cerebrovascular injury, breast function for lactation) risk is greater in children, and adult-derived thresholds would understate harm. For the ovary the direction reverses, with less risk in children and lesser risk again in younger children within the pediatric range.

The within-pediatric gradient matters as much as the child-adult contrast. Younger children carry greater risk for hearing loss and neurocognitive decline, while younger age is associated with lesser risk for ovary and thyroid. A planner treating a toddler and an adolescent with the same posterior fossa field is effectively working with two different constraint sets, and the paper is candid that the field has not settled whether age should enter NTCP models as a continuous variable or as developmental bands.

The central methodological caveat is confounding, and the authors name it directly. Children and adults receiving RT differ in histology, prescription dose, field design and concurrent chemotherapy. A pediatric medulloblastoma survivor and an adult glioma pt differ in far more than age, so an apparent age effect on neurocognition could partly reflect craniospinal fields or chemotherapy exposure rather than developmental sensitivity alone. That should temper confidence in the direction calls where the paper hedges (lung, 'perhaps slightly less') and in any attempt to read the comparisons as causal.

The abstract offers directions only, without dose-volume thresholds or NTCP magnitudes, so the value of this piece is as a map of where to consult the organ-specific PENTEC reports rather than as a source of numbers. Its practical message for planning is that adult constraint tables are a reasonable starting point for some organs and a misleading one for others, and that the pediatric developmental endpoints (musculoskeletal growth, dentition, breast and reproductive development) have no adult analogue at all. What would make this framing wrong is if the observed differences dissolve once treatment paradigm is adjusted for; until age-stratified data with harmonized exposure exist, the comparisons should be read as directional and hypothesis-generating.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Adult QUANTEC/HyTEC constraints do not transfer uniformly: neurocognition, cerebrovascular and breast-lactation risks run greater in children, ovary less. Younger children carry greater hearing and neurocognitive risk, so age at RT should modify how brain and posterior fossa constraints are read.

open_questions: Should age enter NTCP models as continuous or developmental groupings?
Do child vs adult differences persist after adjusting for fields and chemo?

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: AAPM HyTEC literature pooling with logistic NTCP modeling. PubMed search (April 2018) yielded **238 major vessel Dmax values from 6 articles**; two later series with dose-volume data were modeled separately for comparison.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: Grade 3-5 events grouped. **BE** = any bleeding event, radiation or tumor; **CBS** = carotid bleeding without adjacent persistent or progressive disease. Only the Gebhardt data set reports essentially pure CBS.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: SBRT reirradiation, vessel doses expressed in **5 fractions**. Prior course assumed a nominal **70 Gy conventional**, interval approximately ≥6 mo (reported range 2 to 423 mo, median about 2 yr). No model includes the prior dose on its x-axis.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: Pooled Dmax model **TD50 45.7 Gy** (95% CI 39.6-64.9). Only 1 BE occurred at carotid Dmax <30 Gy. With risk-reduction strategies, G3-5 CBS risk was **2.2%** when 1 cm3 exceeded 20 Gy and **<1%** when 0.1 cm3 exceeded 20 Gy in 5 fx.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: A cited systematic review put vessel injury risk at 1.3% to 4.5%. Lower event rates in the Gebhardt alternating-day series vs the earlier Yazici-era cohort suggest the risk-reduction bundle works, but cross-institution and cross-era comparison limits the inference.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents recurrent H&N pts reirradiated with 5-fx SBRT after ~70 Gy prior conventional RT with an interval of roughly ≥6 mo. Does not represent de novo SBRT, a planned SBRT boost, or pts with long life expectancy.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Median follow-up **<2 yr** in all modeled series except Gebhardt survivors (37 mo; 8 mo overall). Carotid contour extent and branch inclusion vary across studies, so only D0.1cc/Dmax pool reliably. Gebhardt doses were summed physically across 1 to 3 courses with no repair factor.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: Authors present the models as general guidance, not risk probabilities. Recurrent H&N pts are **4 to 5 times more likely to die of uncontrolled disease** than of a modern reRT complication, so failing a carotid constraint should not by itself preclude treatment. Proactive stenting is an option when expected bleeding risk exceeds stent risk.

studies.interpretation:
The value of this report lies less in its fitted curves than in what it shows about the evidence behind carotid constraints for SBRT reirradiation. The pooled Dmax model rests on 238 vessel doses from six series, but the events driving the fit are bleeding events that, in all but one data set, cannot be separated from tumor eroding into the vessel. A dose-response curve built on that endpoint conflates two opposite clinical meanings. Bleeding from radiation injury argues for lower vessel dose, while bleeding from persistent disease argues for the opposite, better target coverage up to the vessel wall. The authors acknowledge this, and that tension should govern how a radiation oncologist reads the TD50 of 45.7 Gy: it describes where events cluster in a heterogeneous, largely pre-mitigation literature, not a tolerance dose.

The more decision-relevant thread is the contrast between the earlier Yazici-era data and the Gebhardt/Ling series, which was treated every other day with risk-reduction strategies applied. Event rates there were lower, and the CBS-specific model puts grade 3-5 risk at 2.2% when 1 cm3 exceeds 20 Gy in 5 fractions. That supports alternating-day delivery and carotid volume restriction as working practice. Still, the comparison crosses institutions, eras, endpoint definitions and contouring conventions, and the CBS model rests on 5 events in 4 pts. Because every mitigation was applied as a bundle, no single factor can be credited, and a clinic that adopts only nonconsecutive-day scheduling has no estimate of what it gains.

Several structural gaps limit transfer. Prior dose enters only as an assumed nominal 70 Gy with no per-patient interval, so the models cannot see the variable most reirradiation decisions hinge on. Vessel contour extent and branch inclusion differ across series, which is why only small-volume metrics such as D0.1cc and Dmax pool sensibly; a center contouring a long carotid segment will generate D50% values that do not compare with anyone else's. Median follow-up under 2 years in nearly all series means late vessel events in longer survivors are underrepresented, which matters more as reirradiation selection improves.

The RTOG 3507 constraints (Dmax ≤42 Gy, D50% ≤32 Gy) are offered as a conservative working standard, explicitly nonvalidated, and the authors state that missing them should not by itself rule out treatment. That framing is right. Recurrent H&N pts are described as 4 to 5 times more likely to die of uncontrolled disease than of a reirradiation complication, so a planner who trades gross tumor coverage for carotid sparing may be exchanging a rare toxicity for a likely failure. Circumferential encasement and pre-existing skin necrosis are where that trade turns unfavorable for SBRT, and the report points those pts toward conventional or hyperfractionated retreatment.

The endpoint problem is also how this could be wrong. If a large share of pooled bleeding events were tumor-driven, the true radiation dose response could be flatter than modeled, and current constraints would be overly cautious at the expense of local control. Settling that requires prospective per-patient reporting of composite dose, interval, fractionation schedule and local control adjacent to the vessel, which is the report's own closing argument.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: For 5-fx reRT, carotid Dmax <20 to 30 Gy carried low observed risk, and every-other-day delivery with D0.5cc <20 Gy is the mitigation bundle behind the lowest event rates. RTOG 3507's Dmax ≤42 Gy and D50% ≤32 Gy are nonvalidated guides; circumferential encasement favors conventional or hyperfractionated reRT.

open_questions: Relative contribution of each risk-reduction factor
Carotid tolerance with prior dose and repair included
Role of proactive carotid stenting before SBRT reRT

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Practical contouring guideline pairing trigeminal radio-anatomy (V1/V2/V3 paths, PPF hub, V-VII connections) with imaging review and **Table 2 target volume recommendations**. Consensus process not described in source.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: Unresected macroscopic PNI: **GTV = entire post-contrast enhancement**, **CTV-P1 = GTV + 5 mm** along the nerve. **CTV-P2 ≥30 mm** along the nerve path, skull base often recommended, extended to brainstem with skull base involvement. Resected R1: close margin + 5 mm plus PNI in the whole tumor bed.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: EORTC 22931 included PNI pts and showed concurrent cisplatin improved locoregional control over PORT alone. The Zukauskaite series of 1576 pts treated with primary RT for H&N SCC found most recurrences in the GTV, but excluded ACC, nasopharynx, paranasal sinuses and skin, the sites most at risk of PNI spread.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents H&N SCC and ACC with microscopic or macroscopic trigeminal PNI planned for primary or post-op IMRT. Does not represent facial nerve-only PNI or a validated outcome-based margin.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: The only pattern-of-failure series cited excluded the PNI-prone histology and sites, so the 30 mm CTV-P2 is not failure-validated. No dose prescriptions in the source excerpt, and OAR trade-offs at the skull base are left case-by-case.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The core argument is that imaging undercalls PNI extent, so the low-risk CTV follows the anatomic route rather than visible disease. Whether **≥30 mm and skull base coverage** reduces perineural failure enough to justify brainstem and optic dose is not settled here.

studies.interpretation:
This paper is best read as an anatomic map with a margin convention attached, not as an evidence synthesis. Its value for the planner is the route logic: which division a given primary feeds, where that division exits the skull base, and where the divisions and the facial nerve communicate, with the pterygopalatine fossa as the junction through which a palatal, sinus or nasopharyngeal primary can reach V2, the orbit, the masticator space and the Vidian nerve. That logic is durable and largely independent of the margin numbers.

The margins themselves are where confidence should be lower. The 5 mm expansion from enhancing nerve to CTV-P1 and the 30 mm minimum along the nerve path for CTV-P2 are presented as recommendations, but the source gives no failure data that generated them. The one pattern-of-failure series it cites, Zukauskaite and colleagues in 1576 pts with primary RT for SCC, found most recurrences inside the GTV, and the authors themselves note it excluded ACC, nasopharynx, paranasal sinuses and skin. In other words, the population that supports a tight approach is not the population this guideline is written for, and the population this guideline is written for has no comparable failure analysis in the source.

The strongest part of the argument for generous elective coverage is the imaging section. MRI detects macroscopic PNI with high sensitivity, yet in the two operated series cited it misdefined extent in 5 of 30 and 4 of 36 detected cases, and missed 2 of 38 outright. Pathology shows continuous spread where imaging shows skip lesions. If the visible enhancement is a floor rather than a boundary, then contouring only what enhances will systematically undertreat, and the guideline's choice to follow the anatomic route toward skull base is the logical response. The recommendation for MRI in treatment position and rigid co-registration follows from the same reasoning.

What the paper does not resolve is the cost side. Extending CTV-P2 to skull base, or to brainstem with intracranial involvement, and bilaterally for non-lateralized tumors, pushes target volume into brainstem, brain and optic pathway, and the source leaves that trade to case-by-case judgment without dose guidance. For focal microscopic PNI in SCC, the evidence for adjuvant RT is described as too thin for firm conclusions, so that remains a judgment call rather than a protocol. The particle therapy comment for unresected ACC is explicitly made without randomized support.

The guideline would be wrong, or at least overcautious, if PNI-specific failure mapping in ACC and high-risk-site SCC showed recurrences clustering within a few millimetres of visible enhancement. Until such data exist, it is a reasonable anatomic default whose margins are convention, not measurement.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: MRI misdefined macroscopic PNI extent in 17% and 11% of operated series, and imaging skip lesions understate continuous spread, which is why CTV-P2 runs ≥30 mm along the nerve and often to skull base. Coverage is retrograde by default, antegrade when symptoms or imaging suggest, bilateral for non-lateralized primaries.

open_questions: Pattern-of-failure validation of ≥30 mm nerve-path CTV-P2
Role of particle RT in unresected or residual ACC
Adjuvant RT benefit for focal microscopic PNI alone

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: **Consensus guideline** from cooperative groups including AIRO, DAHANCA, EORTC, GORTEC, NCIC CTG, NRG Oncology and TROG. Evidence base: pathology of resection specimens plus local control after margin-limited transoral surgery.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: **CTV-P1 = GTV-P + 5 mm**, tied to the highest dose (typically 70 Gy in 2 Gy fractions over 7 weeks). **CTV-P2 = GTV-P + 10 mm**, at 50 Gy (2 dose levels) or 60 Gy (3 dose levels, with CTV-P3 at 50 Gy). Both are edited for air, anatomic barriers and uninvolved cartilage, and CTV-P1 always sits inside CTV-P2.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: Per-subsite rules are in the table. Key departures: **no CTV-P2 for T1 glottic**, optional CTV-P2 for small T2 glottic, T1 subglottic and T1 hypopharynx, and a **15 mm cranio-caudal option** for T2-T4 hypopharynx.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Smaller margins are justified by transoral series: a **2-3 mm** mucosal margin gave LC **85-95%** in T1-T2 glottic/supraglottic and **above 90%** in T1-T2 tonsil without PORT. Zanoni et al. put the optimal surgical margin at **2.2 mm** for loco-regional recurrence-free survival.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents primary-setting RT for laryngeal, hypopharyngeal, oropharyngeal and oral cavity SCC. Does not represent post-operative beds or recurrent disease, where prior treatment has altered the anatomy.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Most specimen data come from T1-T2 tumours. Subglottic SCC is **under 5%** of laryngeal SCC, so data there are sparse. Infiltrative borders and tumour budding break the assumption that tumour density falls off with distance from the GTV. The surgical series are highly selected and mostly HPV-positive in the tonsil.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The volume reduction depends on accurate GTV-P delineation, because every margin is measured from it. Where the GTV is uncertain (infiltrative tumours, large inter-observer variability), the 5 mm CTV-P1 has less room for error than older, larger volumes did.

studies.interpretation:
This guideline replaces compartment-style thinking about the primary with a distance-based model: tumour cell density is assumed to fall with distance from the visible GTV, so two concentric rims (5 mm and 10 mm) carry the high and lower dose levels. Everything about its safety depends on that assumption and on the GTV being drawn correctly. The evidence offered is indirect. Resection-specimen pathology shows where microscopic extension stops, and transoral laser and robotic series show that margins of a few millimetres control most early glottic, supraglottic and tonsillar primaries without adjuvant RT. Neither source measures what happens when an RT target is shrunk, which is the question a contouring reader actually faces.

The surgical analogy deserves scrutiny. A surgeon resecting a T1 glottic or tonsillar primary sees the mucosal edge in real time and confirms margins histologically. A radiation oncologist contouring on CT or MRI has neither, and the guideline itself says these series were highly selected and run by high-volume centres. The 10-15% local relapses in those series are attributed to biology rather than margin, which is plausible but not shown. So the transfer from a 2-3 mm surgical margin to a 5 mm CTV-P1 is reasoned rather than demonstrated, and the extra 2-3 mm is in effect an allowance for imaging uncertainty.

The subsite exceptions are where the document earns its keep. Dropping CTV-P2 for T1 glottic tumours reflects how tightly confined early cord lesions are, while the hypopharynx is handled the opposite way: submucosal spread of 20-30 mm cranio-caudally makes a uniform 10 mm expansion inadequate, hence the optional 15 mm. A reader who adopts the 5+5 concept without the hypopharyngeal caveat takes on the risk the guideline itself flags. Subglottic guidance rests on very few data and should be read as expert opinion.

The anatomic editing rules (air, bone, fascia, uninvolved cartilage, adjacent subsites) are where real-world variation will concentrate. Two contours can both be 'GTV-P+10 mm, edited' and still differ substantially at the strap muscles or the thyroid cartilage. The figure atlas narrows that variation, but it does not remove it.

The boundaries are clear: primary setting only, no post-operative bed, no recurrence, and PTV margins left to each centre. The open question is whether pattern-of-failure data from centres using these volumes show marginal recurrences concentrated in infiltrative or HPV-negative tumours, where the density-gradient assumption is weakest.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: The high-dose volume shrinks to GTV-P+5 mm, and T1 glottic primaries get no CTV-P2. Hypopharynx is the exception: submucosal spread up to 20-30 mm supports a 15 mm cranio-caudal CTV-P2, so a uniform 10 mm expansion under-covers it.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Expert **consensus guideline** endorsed by DAHANCA, EORTC, HKNPCSG, NCIC CTG, NCRI, RTOG and TROG. Panel of radiation oncologists, a head and neck surgeon and an anatomist.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Builds on the **Robbins-modified level classification** and maps it to the TNM atlas node groups. The level V cranial limit moves from the sternocleidomastoid/trapezius convergence to the **hyoid bone**, since its uppermost nodes belong to the occipital group (Xb).

analysis_sections.label: Applies to

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Landmarks assume a **neutral head position**; with hyperextension, relationships near the skull base shift (upper edge of C1 suggested over the hard palate for VIIa). Medial retropharyngeal nodes are left out of VIIa by choice.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The value is a **single shared nomenclature** for protocols and multi-institution QA, supported by a 110-section DICOM-RT reference set. Whether the revised edges miss recurrences is untested in the source.

studies.interpretation:
The practical value of this update lies less in any single boundary than in replacing several parallel vocabularies with one. Before it, a radiation oncologist reading a trial protocol could meet the Robbins-modified levels, the TNM atlas node groups, and local conventions for the parotid, retropharyngeal and supraclavicular regions, the last three often without a defined CT edge. The 2013 scheme keeps the familiar I to VI numbering for the surgical neck and appends VII to X for node groups that surgeons rarely dissect but that radiation oncologists routinely have to decide on: retropharyngeal and retro-styloid, parotid, bucco-facial, retroauricular and occipital. Giving those regions a number and a full set of boundaries is what makes them reportable in a protocol and auditable in a plan review.

Several boundary choices read as deliberate trade-offs rather than pure anatomy. The caudal edge of IVa was placed 2 cm above the sternal manubrium because that is roughly where a level IVa dissection stops, so the surgical and radiotherapy definitions now describe the same tissue; the low neck beneath is then split into a medial (IVb) and lateral (Vc) supraclavicular group. Moving the cranial limit of level V down to the hyoid reallocates the uppermost posterior triangle nodes to the occipital group, which matters for a scalp skin primary and trims level V for a mucosal one. Restricting VIIa to the lateral retropharyngeal nodes, and holding VIb's upper edge at the thyroid cartilage except for anterior floor of mouth, tongue tip and lower lip primaries, both narrow default volumes on drainage reasoning rather than outcome data.

That is the main methodological caveat. This is an expert consensus, and the source carries no interobserver agreement figures, no dosimetric comparison against older contours, and no patterns-of-failure series testing whether the new edges miss recurrences. Its authority rests on the breadth of the endorsing groups and the mix of disciplines on the panel, not on validation. A recurrence just outside a revised edge, at the IVa/IVb junction or in a medial retropharyngeal node, is exactly the evidence that would test it, and a reader should weigh such reports against the guideline rather than assume the guideline settles them.

Scope is also narrower than the title implies. The panel explicitly declined to say which levels to treat or at what dose, so the document standardizes the contour and leaves CTV selection to site-specific recommendations and clinical judgment. The landmarks assume a neutral head position; the authors concede that hyperextension shifts relationships near the skull base and suggest the upper edge of C1, rather than the hard palate, as the retropharyngeal limit in that case.

The gain is plainest for trial work, where a shared 110-section DICOM-RT reference set lets multi-institution QA compare like with like. In routine practice it functions as the default atlas, with judgment reserved for the edge cases the authors themselves flag.

analysis_sections.body: Narrative review (Oral Oncology 2018) of the international consensus guidelines for **neck level selection**, **nodal delineation** and **primary-tumor CTV**. No new outcome data; authors declare no conflict of interest.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: The consensus sits between the anatomic school (whole compartments, **2-3 cm** where no barrier) and **DAHANCA geometric 5 + 5 mm** margins. Authors expect smaller volumes than the anatomic approach in all directions, and smaller than DAHANCA mainly axially for T1-T2 tumors; no systematic comparison was performed.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Tighter margins are justified by **surgical pathology series** (infiltration typically within 5 mm) and transoral resections in selected, mostly T1-T2 tumors. The prospective DAHANCA geographic-miss analysis was **still ongoing** at publication.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: Most local failures arise inside the GTV regardless of margin, so the consensus trades volume for morbidity on the premise that **biology, not delineation**, drives relapse. That premise holds only when the GTV comes from full endoscopic and imaging workup.

studies.interpretation:
The core of this review is a change in how the primary-tumor CTV is justified. The anatomic approach (Eisbruch; Grégoire and Daisne; developed in the French literature by Lapeyre) treats microscopic spread as compartmental: once a barrier is breached, the whole compartment is at risk, and where no barrier exists a 2-3 cm margin stands in. DAHANCA started from the opposite premise, that tumor cell density falls with distance from the GTV, and replaced compartments with a fixed 5 mm plus 5 mm expansion edited only for bone and air. The international consensus sits between them, using 5 and 10 mm geometric expansions as the scaffold and then editing for routes of spread and anatomic barriers. By the authors' own estimate, this gives smaller volumes than the anatomic approach in every direction, especially in the oropharynx, and smaller than DAHANCA mainly in the axial plane and mainly for T1-T2 disease.

The evidence for tightening is thinner than the confidence of the recommendation suggests. The pathology series cited show infiltration typically within the first 5 mm, and transoral resections with 2 to 3 mm margins in selected, mostly T1-T2 tumors had low local recurrence without adjuvant RT. Both are surgical, selected and early-stage. Neither says what a 10 mm edited CTV does around a deeply infiltrating primary, such as the T3 base-of-tongue case the authors use for illustration, which is exactly where the volume differences between schools grow large. The strongest RT-specific datum is the three-center Danish analysis: across margins from 0 to 10 mm, recurrences sat mainly within the GTV, local relapse did not track margin, and the few out-of-CTV failures fell inside the 95% isodose. That supports the claim that biology, not geography, drives most in-field failure. It is still a retrospective comparison of centers with different habits, and the prospective DAHANCA geographic-miss analysis was described as ongoing.

A second hinge is the GTV itself. Every geometric margin inherits the GTV's error, which is why the guidance insists on contrast planning CT at 2 mm, endoscopy under general anesthesia, MRI, and PET for larger tumors. A center that adopts the smaller margins without that workup is applying half the consensus. The authors also allow the treating physician to draw a larger GTV when information is missing. That is a reasonable escape valve, and it is also the route by which inter-center variation comes back.

The neck recommendations are less contentious. Selective elective treatment for cN0 and N1, levels II to IVa for pharyngo-laryngeal primaries and I to III for oral cavity, widening to Ib through V for N2a, N2b and N3, follows the predictable drainage data. The p16-positive oropharynx caveat needs care. The authors state there is no data to treat it differently, which is an absence of evidence, not evidence of equivalence, and 8th-edition restaging moves pts across the N categories the tables are keyed to.

The consensus would be wrong if marginal failures rise once smaller volumes are adopted widely, particularly in larger oropharyngeal and hypopharyngeal primaries with submucosal spread. Until a prospective failure-pattern analysis reports, this is a well-reasoned volume reduction resting on pathology and retrospective recurrence mapping, and it is explicitly not validated for the postoperative neck or non-SCC histology.

That supports 5 and 10 mm edited expansions over whole-compartment CTVs, but only with 2 mm contrast planning CT, endoscopy under GA and MRI defining the GTV.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: 90% TCP at **20 Gy/1, 28 Gy/2, 33 Gy/3**, and 40 Gy/5 by extrapolation. Common schedules model to **82% to 96%** 2y LC.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: RTOG 0631 and SC24 randomize spine SBRT against conventional RT on **pain response**, so neither will validate these LC estimates. The authors cite a recent systematic review that favored single-fraction dosing, with the same data-quality limits.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents spinal metastases treated with 1 to 5 fraction SBRT, with prior-RT and RT-naive lesions pooled. Does not represent postoperative SBRT, histology-specific dosing or primary spinal tumors.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: The cord constraint of 10 to 14 Gy/1 **undercovers the epidural PTV**, so delivered dose diverges from prescription exactly where failures cluster. Data span treatments from 2006 to 2018, so changes in imaging, IGRT and target definition are folded into one curve.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The model supports current practice of **18 to 24 Gy/1, 24 Gy/2 and 27 to 30 Gy/3** rather than redefining it. Its main output is a reporting agenda: **Dmin/D95 coverage**, defined CTV and competing-risk LC, so future pooling can model delivered dose.

studies.interpretation:
The value of this analysis is less the curve itself than what the curve cannot see. The model ties 2-year local control to the prescription dose written on the plan, but the authors acknowledge that in spine SBRT the prescription is the dose the tumor is least likely to actually receive at its most dangerous edge. The cord constraint routinely pulls the epidural portion of the PTV below the named isodose, and the epidural space is where these lesions most often fail. So the fitted relationship between prescription and control is partly a relationship between prescription and how much of the target escaped coverage. The single-institution comparison the authors cite, 98% versus 85% two-year control at the same 24 Gy prescription depending on PTV D95, makes the point more sharply than any pooled estimate: within one prescription, coverage spread a gap as wide as the whole difference between 18 and 24 Gy in the model.

That should shape how a reader uses the 82% to 96% range. Moving from 18 to 24 Gy in one fraction looks like a large gain on the curve, but it assumes the extra dose lands where recurrence starts. For a lesion abutting the thecal sac, raising the prescription may mostly raise dose in bone that was already controlled, while the epidural sliver stays capped by the cord. The decision that moves control in that patient may be separation surgery or a cord constraint the reader is willing to relax, not the nominal prescription. The paper frames future cord-tolerance work as a route to better TCP for exactly this reason.

The α/β of 6 Gy deserves similar caution. It comes from a handful of isoeffect comparisons across sparse fractionation data, and the individual estimates ranged from 3 to 12 Gy. Pooled values in 2, 4 and 5 fractions, especially at the 95% level, are extrapolations off that single parameter. Readers comparing a 5-fraction reirradiation schedule against single-fraction de novo treatment are leaning on the least certain part of the model.

The endpoint is also likely biased upward. Actuarial local control that censors at death assumes death is independent of spinal progression, which is implausible in metastatic disease, and the authors explicitly favor cumulative incidence with death as a competing risk. Pooling previously irradiated with unirradiated lesions, and leaving out histology and volume, further blends populations whose control may differ for reasons dose cannot explain.

None of this undermines current practice; the curve lands where most programs already prescribe. What it does not settle is whether single-fraction escalation beats multifraction schedules on therapeutic ratio, or what control looks like after separation surgery, which was not modeled. The randomized spine SBRT trials named here, RTOG 0631 and SC24, are built around pain response, so they will not answer the TCP question either. The durable contribution is the reporting standard: series that publish Dmin or D95 coverage alongside competing-risk control would let the next pooled model fit delivered dose rather than intent.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Coverage moves control more than prescription: in one 811-lesion series at 24 Gy/1, 2y control was 98% with PTV D95 >22.4 Gy vs 85% below 16.5 Gy. Epidural failure next to the cord predominates, so cord-constrained underdosing, not the nominal dose, is the lever.

Single vs multifraction spine SBRT therapeutic ratio
TCP of SBRT after separation surgery

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: HyTEC literature review: PubMed search of hypofractionated SBRT series (usually **1-5 fx**), pooled into **logistic TCP models** fit by maximum likelihood. Not a trial; patient-level data not stated in source.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Published series in **preoperative (neoadjuvant), borderline resectable, and locally advanced** pancreatic cancer. Per-series N, staging and systemic backbone not given in abstract.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: All regimens converted to **3-fraction equivalent doses** with LQ, **α/β = 10 Gy**. Alliance A021501's **33 Gy/5fx** maps to **28.2 Gy/3fx**.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **1-year LC**, modeled without surgery and with margin-negative resection. OS and toxicity outcomes not reported in abstract.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: **Dose response across 25 to 36 Gy** (3-fx equivalent); dose-level LC values in the table above.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Alliance A021501 is the cooperative-group anchor for 5-fx pancreatic SBRT; its schedule lands at a modeled **77%** 1-yr LC, **below the 30 to 36 Gy band** where modeled LC was highest.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents localized pancreatic cancer treated with 1-5 fx SBRT, preop, borderline resectable, or locally advanced. Does not represent conventionally fractionated chemoRT or metastatic disease.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Pooled series inherit each report's LC definition and imaging, and post-SBRT CT response in pancreas is hard to read. Resected-pt LC **>90%** reflects selection into R0 surgery as much as dose.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The model frames dose as the open lever for unresected pts. Whether escalation beyond the A021501 dose is deliverable near duodenum and stomach, and whether 1-yr LC gains move OS, is **not addressed** in the abstract.

studies.interpretation:
The value of this HyTEC analysis is less any single percentage than the common axis it imposes on a literature that lacked one. Pancreatic SBRT has been delivered across 1 to 5 fractions with little agreement on total dose, and converting every regimen to a 3-fraction equivalent lets a reader place a prescription on one curve. On that curve, the schedule chosen for Alliance A021501, 33 Gy in 5 fractions, lands at 28.2 Gy in 3 fractions and a modeled 77% 1-year LC without surgery. That point sits inside the 25 to 36 Gy range where the model still shows dose response, and below the 30 to 36 Gy band associated with ≈79% to 86%. Read plainly, the most visible prospective 5-fraction schedule may not sit on the plateau of the curve.

How much weight that deserves depends on the conversion. LQ with α/β = 10 Gy is a convention, and its behavior at the dose per fraction used in 1 to 3 fraction SBRT is debated. If the model overstates the effect of very large fractions, single- and three-fraction series are credited with more equivalent dose than they deliver, and the slope moves. The logistic fit also inherits whatever LC definition each published series used, and LC in pancreas is hard to score on CT after SBRT because fibrosis and residual mass persist. A pooled curve built from abstract-level outcomes cannot separate dose from era, staging, systemic backbone, or how aggressively each group imaged.

The surgical figure needs a separate read. LC above 90% after margin-negative resection at more than 28 Gy equivalent mixes RT dose with selection: pts who reach R0 resection differ anatomically and biologically from those who do not, and resection removes much of the target whose control is being measured. It says little about whether dose itself contributes once a margin-negative resection is achieved, and nothing about whether dose changes the chance of getting there.

What the analysis does not settle is the question that governs a pancreatic SBRT prescription: whether the increment needed to move from the A021501 point into the upper band is deliverable given duodenum, stomach and bowel proximity, and whether a 1-year LC gain matters in a disease where distant progression usually dominates survival. The title references complication limits, but the abstract here does not report the toxicity side of the trade, so the cost of escalation is not visible from this source. Daily adaptation and OAR-sparing techniques are the natural route to test the hypothesis prospectively.

For practice, this is a framework for locating a chosen dose, not evidence that escalation improves outcomes that matter. A radiation oncologist prescribing 5-fraction SBRT for unresected disease can use it to see that 33 Gy/5fx sits on the rising part of a modeled curve; turning that into a reason to escalate would take a prospective dose comparison with LC, OS and late GI toxicity measured together. The authors' own call for caution is the right register.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: A021501's 33 Gy/5fx maps to 28.2 Gy/3fx and a modeled 77% 1-yr LC without surgery, below the 30 to 36 Gy band at ≈79% to 86%. For unresected pts this frames dose escalation within OAR limits as the open lever, pending prospective dose comparison.

Can escalated pancreatic SBRT doses meet duodenal and gastric constraints?
Is LQ conversion at α/β 10 valid for 1-3 fraction SBRT?

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Spinal cord tolerance data for SBRT were **extracted from published reports, reviewed, and modelled**. No new pt cohort; pooled N and RM event count not given in the abstract.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: **De novo SBRT in 1 to 5 fx**: cord point Dmax at **1% to 5% RM risk** is **12.4 to 14.0 Gy/1fx, 17.0 Gy/2fx, 20.3 Gy/3fx, 23.0 Gy/4fx, 25.3 Gy/5fx**.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: **Re-SBRT** factors associated with lower RM risk: cumulative thecal sac EQD2 Dmax **≤70 Gy**, SBRT thecal sac EQD2 Dmax **≤25 Gy**, SBRT-to-cumulative Dmax ratio **≤0.5**, and interval **≥5 months** (EQD2 with α/β 2).

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: QUANTEC framed cord tolerance largely around conventional fractionation; this report moves the question to the **1 to 5 fx regimens** used in spine SBRT, and adds a reirradiation framework QUANTEC did not provide.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents pts receiving 1 to 5 fx spine SBRT, de novo or as reirradiation. Does not represent conventionally fractionated cord exposure.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Built on **published series, not complete institutional cohorts** with dosimetry in pts with and without RM. Re-SBRT thresholds are **associations**, not modelled tolerance doses, and rest on LQ conversion at SBRT dose per fraction.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: Gives a defensible, citable cord Dmax per fraction number and a **combined** reirradiation rule set. A plan inside all four re-SBRT thresholds sits in the lower-risk region of reported experience, which is **not the same as proven safe**.

studies.interpretation:
These values have become the working cord constraints for spine SBRT, and their main contribution is replacing center-by-center extrapolation from conventional fractionation with limits derived from hypofractionated exposures themselves. QUANTEC addressed cord tolerance largely in the conventional setting; this report moves the question to the 1 to 5 fraction regimens that dominate spine metastasis practice. The de novo table has the shape one expects if dose per fraction drives risk: each added fraction buys a progressively smaller increment in tolerated point dose, and the single-fraction value is the only one expressed as a range (12.4 to 14.0 Gy), which is where uncertainty matters most because single-fraction radiosurgery is where planners push hardest against the cord.

The methodology should temper how literally those numbers are read. The source is published reports, extracted and modelled, not pooled individual-pt dosimetry. Radiation myelopathy is rare, so any model fit depends heavily on a small number of events, and published series are not a random sample of institutional experience. The authors' own closing call, for complete institutional cohorts with dosimetric data in pts with and without myelopathy, points at the weak point: the denominator of pts who received a known cord dose and did not develop myelopathy is what refines a dose-response curve, and that is what published reports tend to omit. Each value is also attached to a 1% to 5% risk band rather than a point risk, so these are planning thresholds, not calibrated probabilities. Point Dmax is sensitive to contouring convention, image fusion and planning resolution, and the abstract does not state the cord definition behind the de novo values, so transfer depends on whether a center contours the way the underlying series did.

The reirradiation half is a different kind of evidence. Rather than modelled tolerance doses, it lists factors associated with lower risk: a cumulative thecal sac EQD2 Dmax ≤70 Gy, an SBRT-course thecal sac EQD2 Dmax ≤25 Gy, an SBRT-to-cumulative ratio ≤0.5, and at least 5 months between courses. These are expressed through linear-quadratic conversion with an α/β of 2, and the validity of LQ scaling at SBRT dose per fraction is itself debated, so the EQD2 thresholds function partly as a shared bookkeeping convention. The ratio criterion is the most specific idea here: it says the SBRT course should not dominate the cumulative cord exposure, which is a structural constraint rather than a dose ceiling. A plan meeting all four sits within reported lower-risk experience; a plan exceeding one is outside that experience, not demonstrated unsafe.

What this changes is the defensibility of plan acceptance and the specificity of consent: a 1% to 5% band can be stated rather than improvised. What it leaves open is whether trading higher cord dose for epidural disease coverage is ever worthwhile, how concurrent systemic therapy alters tolerance (not addressed in the abstract), and whether complete dosimetric cohorts will move these limits. The estimates would be wrong if such cohorts showed myelopathy clustering below these Dmax values, particularly in sequential or short-interval courses.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Reirradiation now has a four-part thecal sac rule set: cumulative EQD2 Dmax ≤70 Gy, SBRT-course EQD2 Dmax ≤25 Gy, SBRT-to-cumulative ratio ≤0.5, and ≥5 months between courses. De novo cord Dmax per fraction number (12.4 to 14.0 Gy/1fx to 25.3 Gy/5fx) anchors plan acceptance at a stated 1% to 5% risk band.

Validity of the re-SBRT ratio and interval thresholds

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: AAPM WGSBRT HyTEC pooled study-level analysis of PubMed series published Jan 1995 to Sep 2017. **56 of 2951** screened manuscripts had usable dose-volume data, covering **13,929 brain metastases**. Logistic TCP models were weighted by the number of tumors with follow-up.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Eligible series had **≥10 pts** per stratified group and reported margin dose, fractionation and size with **≥1-yr actuarial LC**. Most common primaries were lung, melanoma, RCC and breast; most pts were RPA class II where reported. In about half the studies, a median 44% (range 6.9%-100%) had WBRT before or within 1 month of SRS.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: Median margin dose **20 Gy in 1 fx** (range 13-32 Gy in 1-5 fx); median GTV-PTV margin 1 mm (range 0-3). Half the studies predominantly used GK, the rest LINAC, robotic or tomotherapy. Size bins follow RTOG 90-05: ≤20, 21-30, 31-40 mm.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **Primary: LC per metastasis**, most often a >20% diameter increase from the pre-SRS baseline. OS per pt from SRS when reported.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: Models used **α/β 20 Gy** for tumor; reaching 80% 1-yr LC required SFED **19.6 Gy** (medium) and **21.4 Gy** (large).

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: RTOG 90-05 set single-fraction MTDs of 24, 18 and 15 Gy by size in previously irradiated pts, with 11% 2-yr actuarial necrosis and in-field control of about 50%. This model shows those MTDs give **only 75% and ~69% LC** above 20 mm. It extends the 2011 Wiggenraad pooled model, which rested on 12 data points from 11 papers.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents adults with intact brain mets treated with SRS or 3-5 fx fSRS without concurrent systemic therapy. Does not represent postoperative cavities, pediatric pts, or SRS delivered alongside modern IO or targeted therapy.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: LC definitions varied and were mostly MRI-based, so pseudoprogression could inflate failure, while death-censored actuarial estimates could overstate control. Prior WBRT was recorded only as binary, with no cumulative dose. Histology was not stratified outside 4 melanoma-only studies.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: For small non-melanoma lesions, 18 Gy looks adequate, which **argues against reflexive escalation to 24 Gy**; toxicity is outside this TCP analysis. Above 20 mm, necrosis limits single-fraction dose, so fractionation is the lever, but the size of that gain remains a cross-study estimate.

studies.interpretation:
The value of this analysis is calibration rather than discovery. Most single-fraction SRS prescribing for brain metastases still descends from RTOG 90-05, a phase 1 dose-escalation trial in previously irradiated pts whose endpoint was toxicity, not tumor control. Its size-tiered MTDs became de facto prescriptions even though that trial's in-field control estimate was roughly 50%. HyTEC asks the question 90-05 never did: what local control do those doses buy? Across 56 series the answer splits at 20 mm. Below that size, 18 Gy already sits above 85% modeled 1-yr LC, so pushing toward 24 Gy buys a real but modest increment for most histologies. Above 20 mm, the 90-05 MTDs deliver about 75% and 69% 1-yr LC for medium and large lesions. That is the gap fractionation is meant to close.

The fractionation argument is the most clinically useful part of the paper and also the most fragile. The α/β near 20 Gy comes from study-level points pooled across institutions, platforms, margins and eras. Medium and large tumors had to be combined because almost all small-tumor data were single-fraction. A high tumor α/β paired with α/β 2 for normal brain is what makes 3-5 fx attractive on paper: tumor SFED rises while brain SFED falls. The 2-yr large-tumor comparison is the cleanest empirical signal, with 7 of 8 fractionated points above 60%. Still, it compares different series, not randomised arms. The OS imbalance favoring fractionated data points shows the populations differ, and death-censored actuarial LC is sensitive to exactly that kind of difference. The model cannot adjust for case mix, era or platform, so the direction is more defensible than the magnitude.

Measurement cuts both ways. Most failures were defined on MRI, without pathology. Higher single-fraction doses to larger lesions are where treatment effect and pseudoprogression are most likely to be scored as recurrence. If that misclassification concentrated in single-fraction large-tumor series, the single-fraction curves would understate true control, and some of the apparent fractionation benefit would be a reading artifact. If instead censoring at death mainly flattered the series with shorter survival, the bias could run the other way. Neither direction can be resolved from published aggregates, which is why the authors call for per-lesion reporting.

The melanoma finding deserves attention and caution in equal measure. The curve is the steepest in the analysis, with 18 Gy modeling poorly and roughly 24 Gy approaching 95%. But it rests on 4 studies, all small tumors and all single-fraction, so the steepness itself is uncertain. The defensible read is that melanoma needs more dose than the small-lesion default, not the exact control rate at any one dose.

What this does not settle matters as much as what it does. Postoperative cavities were excluded for lack of data, and the authors note a randomised comparison showing lower cavity control with SRS than with WBRT, which they attribute to delineation rather than dose. The pooled series are SRS alone, while modern pts often stay on IO or targeted therapy through SRS, which may shift the dose-response. Toxicity sits outside this TCP paper, so the therapeutic-ratio case for fSRS here is LQ arithmetic, not measured necrosis. There is still no randomised trial comparing fractionation schemes for 2-4 cm lesions, and that is the experiment that would confirm or overturn the model.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Above 20 mm, single-fraction RTOG 90-05 MTDs give only 75% and ~69% 1-yr LC, and large-tumor 2-yr LC never passed 60% with a single fraction, while 7 of 8 fractionated points did. That supports 27-35 Gy in 3-5 fx for 21-40 mm lesions; melanoma needs more than the 18 Gy small-lesion default.

sites.intro: ESTRO ACROP LA-NSCLC: FDG-PET-CT mandatory, pre-induction involved nodes stay in GTV, further elective nodal CTV discouraged.

studies.name: ESTRO ACROP target volume guidelines, locally advanced NSCLC
studies.tldr: Consensus M/R/O/D rules for LA-NSCLC volumes: FDG-PET-CT mandatory, all pre-induction involved nodes in GTV, CTV GTV + 5-8 mm, elective nodal CTV discouraged.

details.text: 🔍 Key recommendations by tier (M mandatory · R recommended · O optional · D discouraged)

rows: PET-CT before induction; repeat contrast chest CT before RT
Treatment position, 2-3 mm slices, cricoid to mid abdomen
All pre-chemo involved nodes/stations, even if resolved on imaging
GTV + 5-8 mm, edited to anatomic barriers
Whole involved station (Option 1) or geometric 5-8 mm (Option 2)
Individual basis on baseline shift / anatomic change

details: 🔍 PET-positive, EBUS/EUS-negative nodes go in the GTV: endoscopic false-negative rates are high
🔍 PET-positive node omitted only with a clear benign biopsy explanation or negative mediastinoscopy
🔍 Uncertain FDG-avid mediastinal node: include rather than exclude

details.text: 🔍 Motion-management options
subdetails: ITV from all 4D-CT phase CTVs, or CTV on MIP
Mid-ventilation or mid-position CT with van Herk margin
Gating or tracking with system-specific PTV margins

details: 🔍 PORT CTV: resected involved mediastinal regions, bronchial stump, ipsilateral hilum, stations 4 and 7
🔍 Mandatory OARs: lungs, whole heart, oesophagus, spinal canal PRV; substructures optional
⚠️ Two nodal CTV options endorsed without a stated failure-pattern comparison between them
⚠️ Excerpt reports no per-item vote counts or evidence grading behind each tier
studies.significance: The nodal GTV rules carry the RT weight: every node involved before induction chemo stays in the GTV even after radiographic resolution (M), and PET-avid but EBUS/EUS-negative nodes stay in. Nodal CTV may be whole-station or a geometric 5-8 mm expansion, while elective coverage beyond hilum and adjacent stations is discouraged.
studies.monday_clinic: In locally advanced NSCLC with an FDG-avid mediastinal node that is EBUS/EUS-negative, this supports keeping it in the GTV unless a benign biopsy explanation or negative mediastinoscopy exists; it does not address SBRT planning, where its conventional-fractionation OAR set does not apply.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Structured committee questionnaire, then consensus discussion and **voting**, with each item sorted into **Mandatory, Recommended, Optional or Discouraged**. Literature referencing was added during writing, after the vote.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: Primary CTV is **GTV + 5-8 mm**, anatomically edited. Nodal CTV is either the **whole involved station** or a **geometric 5-8 mm** expansion; elective inclusion beyond the hilum and adjacent stations is **discouraged**. PTV margins follow ICRU, ideally department-quantified, and are anisotropic where primary and nodal motion differ.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: The nodal GTV algorithm adapts Peeters' prevalence-based model combining CT, PET and E(B)US. Station-based CTV is supported by reference to large multicentre trials with acceptable out-field mediastinal recurrence, which the excerpt does not name.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents curative-intent conventionally fractionated or moderately hypofractionated RT or chemo-RT for locally advanced NSCLC, with PORT by analogy. Does not represent SBRT planning, where trachea, proximal bronchial tree and chest wall contouring become necessary.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: A **mandatory** label on contrast CT and one on a CTV margin read identically despite very different evidentiary support. The **5-8 mm** range lets two compliant centres produce materially different volumes.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The firm positions guard against mediastinal geographic miss, accepting extra oesophageal and lung dose. The open choice between nodal CTV options is permission to use either, not evidence that they are equivalent.

studies.interpretation:
This document is less an evidence synthesis than a codification of how experienced European thoracic centres were already contouring, and its value is that it makes the defaults explicit and auditable. Its firmest positions are the ones that protect against geographic miss in the mediastinum. Every node involved before induction chemotherapy stays in the GTV even after it disappears on imaging, and a PET-avid node stays in despite a negative EBUS or EUS because endoscopic sampling misses disease too often. Both are asymmetric bets. They accept additional dose to oesophagus and lung in exchange for avoiding a marginal or out-field nodal failure, and the panel signalled how it weighed that trade by making the post-induction rule mandatory.

The nodal CTV is where the guideline declines to choose. Permitting either whole-station coverage or a geometric 5-8 mm expansion legitimises two practices that can produce quite different volumes for the same patient. The support offered for station-based coverage is a reference to large multicentre trials without unacceptable out-field mediastinal recurrence, which shows the approach is tolerable, not that it beats the smaller volume. A reader should treat the two options as permission rather than evidence of equivalence. The firmer line is the negative one: elective nodal coverage beyond the hilum and neighbouring stations is discouraged, consistent with the field's long move toward involved-field treatment.

Methodologically, the recommendations come from a questionnaire, committee discussion and a vote, with referencing added afterward. The excerpt reports no panel size, no per-item agreement and no link between a tier and the strength of the underlying data. That matters because the tiers flatten very different kinds of claim. A mandatory diagnostic contrast CT rests on obvious staging logic; a mandatory CTV margin range is a judgement about microscopic extension that the cited literature supports only loosely. The range itself is wide enough that two compliant departments can generate materially different CTVs, which limits its usefulness as a trial QA standard.

Transferability is bounded by fractionation. The OAR list is built for conventional or moderately hypofractionated schedules and explicitly drops trachea, proximal bronchial tree, great vessels and chest wall, so it is the wrong template for SBRT or for hypofractionation aggressive enough that central structures become dose-limiting. Cardiac substructures are optional, a position that reads as conservative given how much attention heart dose has drawn in thoracic RT. The guideline was also written as consolidation immunotherapy after chemoRT was entering practice; where lung and heart sparing carry more weight, the motion-management and anisotropic margin guidance arguably matters more, though the document does not address that setting.

The guideline would be wrong in a useful way if station-based and geometric nodal CTVs turned out to give similar out-field failure, since the larger volume's toxicity cost would then be unearned, or if PET-guided nodal GTVs after induction proved to under-cover disease that pre-treatment sampling missed.

papers.title: Modeling clinical outcomes in radiotherapy: NTCP, TCP and the “TECs”
papers.abstract: Abstract Radiation therapy is a double‐edged sword which damages both tumor and normal cells. Achieving treatments with high tumor control probability (TCP) yet low normal tissue complication probability (NTCP) is often a struggle because we rarely have a unified understanding of the dosimetric and clinical correlates of the desired outcomes. I am fortunate to have participated in some of these struggles, including analyzing and using in‐house data and being involved in the AAPM and ASTRO “TEC” projects—QUANTEC (Quantitatie Analysis of Normal Tissue Effects in the Clinic), HyTEC (Hypofractionated Treatment Effects in the Clinic) and PENTEC (Pediatric Normal Tissue Effects in the Clinic).

papers.title: Comparison of Risks of Late Effects From Radiation Therapy in Children Versus Adults: Insights From the QUANTEC, HyTEC, and PENTEC Efforts
papers.abstract: Pediatric Normal Tissue Effects in the Clinic (PENTEC) seeks to refine quantitative radiation dose-volume relationships for normal-tissue complication probabilities (NTCPs) in survivors of pediatric cancer. This article summarizes the evolution of PENTEC and compares it with similar adult-focused efforts (eg, Quantitative Analysis of Normal Tissue Effects in the Clinic [QUANTEC] and Hypofractionated Treatment Effects in the Clinic [HyTEC]) with respect to content, oversight, support, scope, and methodology of literature review. It then summarizes key organ-specific findings from PENTEC in an attempt to compare NTCP estimates in children versus adults. In brief, select normal-tissue risks within developing organs and tissues (eg, maldevelopment of musculoskeletal tissue, teeth, breasts, and reproductive organs) are primarily relevant only in children. For some organs and tissues, children appear to have similar (eg, brain for necrosis, optic apparatus, parotid gland, liver), greater (eg, brain for neurocognition, cerebrovascular, breast for lactation), less (ovary), or perhaps slightly less (eg, lung) risks of toxicity versus adults. Similarly, even within the broad pediatric age range (including adolescence), for some endpoints, younger children have greater (eg, hearing and brain for neurocognition) or lesser (eg, ovary, thyroid) risks of radiation-associated toxicities. NTCP comparisons in adults versus children are often confounded by marked differences in treatment paradigms that expose normal tissues to radiation (ie, cancer types, prescribed radiation therapy dose and fields, and chemotherapy agents used). To add to the complexity, it is unclear if age is best analyzed as a continuous variable versus with age groupings (eg, infants, young children, adolescents, young adults, middle-aged adults, older adults). Further work is needed to better understand the complex manner in which age and developmental status affect risk.

papers.title: Biological Principles of Stereotactic Body Radiation Therapy (SBRT) and Stereotactic Radiation Surgery (SRS): Indirect Cell Death
papers.abstract: Purpose To review the radiobiological mechanisms of stereotactic body radiation therapy stereotactic body radiation therapy (SBRT) and stereotactic radiation surgery (SRS). Methods and materials We reviewed previous reports and recent observations on the effects of high-dose irradiation on tumor cell survival, tumor vasculature, and antitumor immunity. We then assessed the potential implications of these biological changes associated with SBRT and SRS. Results Irradiation with doses higher than approximately 10 Gy/fraction causes significant vascular injury in tumors, leading to secondary tumor cell death. Irradiation of tumors with high doses has also been reported to increase the antitumor immunity, and various approaches are being investigated to further elevate antitumor immunity. The mechanism of normal tissue damage by high-dose irradiation needs to be further investigated. Conclusions In addition to directly killing tumor cells, high-dose irradiation used in SBRT and SRS induces indirect tumor cell death via vascular damage and antitumor immunity. Further studies are warranted to better understand the biological mechanisms underlying the high efficacy of clinical SBRT and SRS and to further improve the efficacy of SBRT and SRS.

papers.title: Initial Data Pooling for Radiation Dose-Volume Tolerance for Carotid Artery Blowout and Other Bleeding Events in Hypofractionated Head and Neck Retreatments
papers.abstract: Purpose Dose-volume data for injury to carotid artery and other major vessels in stereotactic body radiation therapy (SBRT)/SABR head and neck reirradiation were reviewed, modeled, and summarized. Methods and materials A PubMed search of the English-language literature (stereotactic and carotid and radiation) in April 2018 found 238 major vessel maximum point doses in 6 articles that were pooled for logistic modeling. Two subsequent studies with dose-volume major vessel data were modeled separately for comparison. Attempts were made to separate carotid blowout syndrome from other bleeding events (BE) in the analysis, but we acknowledge that all except 1 data set has some element of BE interspersed. Results Prior radiation therapy (RT) dose was not uniformly reported per patient in the studies included, but a course on the order of conventionally fractionated 70 Gy was considered for the purposes of the analysis (with an approximately ≥6-month estimated interval between prior and subsequent treatment in most cases). Factors likely associated with reduced risk of BE include nonconsecutive daily treatment, lower extent of circumferential tumor involvement around the vessel, and no surgical manipulation before or after SBRT. Conclusions Initial data pooling for reirradiation involving the carotid artery resulted in 3 preliminary models compared in this Hypofractionated Treatment Effects in the Clinic (HyTEC) report. More recent experiences with alternating fractionation schedules and additional risk-reduction strategies are also presented. Complications data for the most critical structures such as spinal cord and carotid artery are so limited that they cannot be viewed as strong conclusions of probability of risk, but rather, as a general guideline for consideration. There is a great need for better reporting standards as noted in the High Dose per Fraction, Hypofractionated Treatment Effects in the Clinic introductory paper.

papers.title: Maximizing Tumor Control and Limiting Complications With Stereotactic Body Radiation Therapy for Pancreatic Cancer
papers.abstract: Purpose Stereotactic body radiation therapy (SBRT) and stereotactic ablative body radiation therapy is being increasingly used for pancreatic cancer (PCa), particularly in patients with locally advanced and borderline resectable disease. A wide variety of dose fractionation schemes have been reported in the literature. This HyTEC review uses tumor control probability models to evaluate the comparative effectiveness of the various SBRT treatment regimens used in the treatment of patients with localized PCa. Methods and materials A PubMed search was performed to review the published literature on the use of hypofractionated SBRT (usually in 1-5 fractions) for PCa in various clinical scenarios (eg, preoperative [neoadjuvant], borderline resectable, and locally advanced PCa). The linear quadratic model with α/β= 10 Gy was used to address differences in fractionation. Logistic tumor control probability models were generated using maximum likelihood parameter fitting. Results After converting to 3-fraction equivalent doses, the pooled reported data and associated models suggests that 1-year local control (LC) without surgery is ≈79% to 86% after the equivalent of 30 to 36 Gy in 3 fractions, showing a dose response in the range of 25 to 36 Gy, and decreasing to less than 70% 1-year LC at doses below 24 Gy in 3 fractions. The 33 Gy in 5 fraction regimen (Alliance A021501) corresponds to 28.2 Gy in 3 fractions, for which the HyTEC pooled model had 77% 1-year LC without surgery. Above an equivalent dose of 28 Gy in 3 fractions, with margin-negative resection the 1-year LC exceeded 90%. Conclusions Pooled analyses of reported tumor control probabilities for commonly used SBRT dose-fractionation schedules for PCa suggests a dose response. These findings should be viewed with caution given the challenges and limitations of this review. Additional data are needed to better understand the dose or fractionation-response of SBRT for PCa.

papers.title: Stereotactic Body Radiation Therapy for Spinal Metastases: Tumor Control Probability Analyses and Recommended Reporting Standards
papers.abstract: Purpose We sought to investigate the tumor control probability (TCP) of spinal metastases treated with stereotactic body radiation therapy (SBRT) in 1 to 5 fractions. Methods and materials PubMed-indexed articles from 1995 to 2018 were eligible for data extraction if they contained SBRT dosimetric details correlated with actuarial 2-year local tumor control rates. Logistic dose-response models of collected data were compared in terms of physical dose and 3-fraction equivalent dose. Results Data were extracted from 24 articles with 2619 spinal metastases. Physical dose TCP modeling of 2-year local tumor control from the single-fraction data were compared with data from 2 to 5 fractions, resulting in an estimated α/β = 6 Gy, and this was used to pool data. Acknowledging the uncertainty intrinsic to the data extraction and modeling process, the 90% TCP corresponded to 20 Gy in 1 fraction, 28 Gy in 2 fractions, 33 Gy in 3 fractions, and (with extrapolation) 40 Gy in 5 fractions. The estimated TCP for common fractionation schemes was 82% at 18 Gy, 90% for 20 Gy, and 96% for 24 Gy in a single fraction, 82% for 24 Gy in 2 fractions, and 78% for 27 Gy in 3 fractions. Conclusions Spinal SBRT with the most common fractionation schemes yields 2-year estimates of local control of 82% to 96%. Given the heterogeneity in the tumor control estimates extracted from the literature, with variability in reporting of dosimetry data and the definition of and statistical methods of reporting tumor control, care should be taken interpreting the resultant model-based estimates. Depending on the clinical intent, the improved TCP with higher dose regimens should be weighed against the potential risks for greater toxicity. We encourage future reports to provide full dosimetric data correlated with tumor local control to allow future efforts of modeling pooled data.

papers.title: Tumor Control Probability of Radiosurgery and Fractionated Stereotactic Radiosurgery for Brain Metastases
papers.abstract: Purpose As part of the American Association of Physicists in Medicine Working Group on Stereotactic Body Radiotherapy, tumor control probability (TCP) after stereotactic radiosurgery (SRS) and fractionated stereotactic radiosurgery (fSRS) for brain metastases was modeled based on pooled dosimetric and clinical data from published English-language literature. Methods and materials PubMed-indexed studies published between January 1995 and September 2017 were used to evaluate dosimetric and clinical predictors of TCP after SRS or fSRS for brain metastases. Eligible studies had ≥10 patients and included detailed dose-fractionation data with corresponding ≥1-year local control (LC) data, typically evaluated as a >20% increase in diameter of the targeted lesion using the pre-SRS diameter as a reference. Results Of 2951 potentially eligible manuscripts, 56 included sufficient dose-volume data for analyses. Accepting that necrosis and pseudoprogression can complicate the assessment of LC, for tumors ≤20 mm, single-fraction doses of 18 and 24 Gy corresponded with >85% and 95% 1-year LC rates, respectively. For tumors 21 to 30 mm, an 18 Gy single-fraction dose was associated with 75% LC. For tumors 31 to 40 mm, a 15 Gy single-fraction dose yielded ∼69% LC. For 3- to 5-fraction fSRS using doses in the range of 27 to 35 Gy, 80% 1-year LC has been achieved for tumors of 21 to 40 mm in diameter. Conclusions TCP for SRS and fSRS are presented. For small lesions ≤20 mm, single doses of ≈18 Gy appear generally associated with excellent rates of LC; for melanoma, higher doses seem warranted. For larger lesions >20 mm, local control rates appear to be ≈ 70% to 75% with usual doses of 15 to 18 Gy, and in this setting, fSRS regimens should be considered. Greater consistency in reporting of dosimetric and LC data is needed to facilitate future pooled analyses. As systemic and biologic therapies evolve, updated analyses will be needed to further assess the necessity, efficacy, and toxicity of SRS and fSRS.

papers.title: Spinal Cord Dose Tolerance to Stereotactic Body Radiation Therapy
papers.abstract: Spinal cord tolerance data for stereotactic body radiation therapy (SBRT) were extracted from published reports, reviewed, and modelled. For de novo SBRT delivered in 1 to 5 fractions, the following spinal cord point maximum doses (D max ) are estimated to be associated with a 1% to 5% risk of radiation myelopathy (RM): 12.4 to 14.0 Gy in 1 fraction, 17.0 Gy in 2 fractions, 20.3 Gy in 3 fractions, 23.0 Gy in 4 fractions, and 25.3 Gy in 5 fractions. For reirradiation SBRT delivered in 1 to 5 fractions, reported factors associated with a lower risk of RM include cumulative thecal sac equivalent dose in 2 Gy fractions with an alpha/beta of 2 (EQD2 2 ) D max ≤70 Gy; SBRT thecal sac EQD2 2 D max ≤25 Gy, thecal sac SBRT EQD2 2 D max to cumulative EQD2 2 D max ratio ≤0.5, and a minimum time interval to reirradiation of ≥5 months. Larger studies containing complete institutional cohorts with dosimetric data of patients treated with spine SBRT, with and without RM, are required to refine RM risk estimates.
